bio: God is the supreme being of the Bible, introduced in its first verse as the creator of the heaven and the earth (Gen 1:1). As Easton's Bible Dictionary notes, the Bible assumes his existence rather than arguing for it. In the King James Version, the Hebrew name Jehovah is usually rendered "LORD" in small capitals, while "God" translates the Hebrew El and Elohim. Other titles include Almighty, Lord of hosts, Father and Judge. Throughout the Old Testament he speaks to Moses, Joshua and the prophets, gives Israel his law, and directs events among the nations, stirring up Cyrus of Persia and handing Jehoiakim over to Babylon (Ezra 1:1; Dan 1:2). In the New Testament Jesus is called the Son of…

Jesus Christ is the central figure of the New Testament. "Jesus" is the Greek form of Joshua, meaning "the LORD saves," and "Christ" is the Greek equivalent of "Messiah," meaning "anointed." Matthew traces his descent from Abraham and David through the tribe of Judah (Matt 1:1). He was born in Bethlehem to Mary, the wife of Joseph, about 4 BC by inference from context. He grew up in Nazareth and had brothers named James, Joses, Jude and Simon. After John baptized him, he taught and healed mainly in Galilee and then went to Jerusalem, where he was crucified about AD 30. The Gospels report that he rose on the third day and ascended to heaven (Luke 24:46). John calls him the Word (John 1:1),…

Jacob (Israel) was the son of Isaac and Rebekah and the younger twin of Esau. He was born holding his brother's heel, which gave him his name (Gen 25:26), and Gen 32:28 records that God later renamed him Israel. By Leah, Rachel and their servants Bilhah and Zilpah he had twelve sons, the ancestors of Israel's tribes, and a daughter, Dinah. Late in life he moved his household to Egypt, where his son Joseph held office, and he died there (Exod 1:1). By inference from context, this entry dates his life to about 1836–1689 BC. He gave Joseph land near Sychar in Samaria (John 4:5). His two names became names for the whole nation, as in "the children of Israel" and "the house of Jacob" (Jer 2:4;…

David was the son of Jesse of Bethlehem, of the tribe of Judah, and the great-grandson of Obed, son of Ruth (Ruth 4:17). 1 Chr 2:15 lists him as Jesse's seventh son. Samuel anointed him as a youth. He later fled from King Saul, led a band of followers and lived for a time at Ziklag. After Saul's death he became king, first at Hebron and then over all Israel from Jerusalem, the "city of David." His power reached as far as Damascus. The account of his family includes his wife Michal, conflict among his sons Amnon and Absalom, and the succession of his son Solomon. He organized the temple singers and is credited with many psalms. Later kings were measured against him, prophets spoke of a…

Moses was the Israelite leader and prophet through whom God brought Israel out of Egypt and gave them the law. A Levite, son of Amram and Jochebed and brother of Aaron and Miriam, he was born in Egypt and raised by Pharaoh's daughter, who named him because she "drew him out of the water." He married Zipporah and had two sons, Gershom and Eliezer. With Aaron he confronted Pharaoh, led the people through the wilderness, received the commandments at Sinai (Horeb), and oversaw the building of the tabernacle. He died on Mount Nebo, and his assistant Joshua succeeded him. Later scripture constantly cites "the law of Moses," and Jewish and Christian tradition credits him with the first five books…

Aaron was the son of Amram and Jochebed, of the tribe of Levi, the brother of Moses and Miriam, and Israel's first high priest. Because he spoke well, God appointed him to speak for Moses before Pharaoh, and the two brothers led Israel out of Egypt (Exod 4:14; 7:1). At Sinai he went partway up the mountain with the elders. While Moses was away, he gave in to the people's demand and made the golden calf, and Moses prayed for him. He and his sons were then consecrated as priests, wearing holy garments and offering sacrifices at the tabernacle. After a challenge to his authority, his rod was kept before the testimony as a sign of his appointment. He married Elisheba and had four sons: Nadab,…

Abraham, first called Abram, was the son of Terah and brother of Nahor and Haran (Gen 11:26). God brought him out of Ur of the Chaldees and renamed him Abraham (Neh 9:7; 1 Chr 1:27), a name Hitchcock's Bible Names explains as "father of a great multitude." He settled in Canaan while his nephew Lot moved toward Sodom (Gen 13:12). His wife Sarah bore him Isaac in old age (Gen 21:7). Sarah's maid Hagar bore Ishmael, and Keturah bore six more sons. God promised that all nations would be blessed in him (Gen 18:18) and swore to give the land to his descendants (Exod 33:1). He was tested by being told to offer Isaac (Heb 11:17) and bought a burial cave from the sons of Heth (Gen 23:20). Later…

Solomon was the son of David and Bathsheba, born in Jerusalem, and was chosen by David from among his many sons to succeed him as king of Israel (1 Chr 3:5; 1 Chr 28:5). According to 2 Sam 12:25, the prophet Nathan gave him the name Jedidiah, "beloved of the LORD." He was made king while David was still alive, even though his half-brother Adonijah was trying to take the throne (1 Kgs 1:10, 37). In his fourth year he began building the temple in Jerusalem (1 Kgs 6:1). He also built a royal palace, with the help of Hiram king of Tyre. His reign was remembered for its wealth, trade and wisdom, which drew the queen of Sheba to visit him (1 Kgs 10:10; Matt 12:42). In old age his foreign wives…

Saul, son of Kish of the tribe of Benjamin, was the first king of Israel. Described as unusually tall and handsome, he was pointed out to the prophet Samuel as the man who would reign, and was later chosen by lot from Benjamin (1 Sam 9:2; 9:17; 10:21). His home was Gibeah, called “Gibeah of Saul.” He fought the Philistines alongside his son Jonathan and campaigned against the Amalekites, after which Samuel confronted him over the LORD’s command. David entered his service and killed Goliath, but Saul grew jealous of David’s fame, tried to kill him, and pursued him through the wilderness. Facing a Philistine attack, he consulted a medium at Endor. He was wounded by archers and died on Mount…

The Holy Spirit, also called the Spirit of God, the Spirit of the LORD, the Holy Ghost and the Comforter, is God's Spirit as presented throughout the Bible. He moves over the waters at creation (Gen 1:2), comes upon judges such as Othniel, speaks through prophets and David, and carries prophets from place to place (Judg 3:10; 2 Sam 23:2; 1 Kgs 18:12). In the Gospels Mary conceives Jesus by the Holy Ghost, and the Spirit descends on Jesus like a dove (Matt 1:18; John 1:32). Jesus promises the Spirit to his disciples, who receive him at Pentecost. In Acts he guides their preaching and missions. The epistles describe the Spirit as given to believers and dwelling in them (Rom 5:5; 2 Tim 1:14).…

Judah (patriarch) was the fourth son of Jacob and Leah. She named him from her words "Now will I praise the LORD" (Gen 29:35). His birth is placed about 1755 BC, by inference from context. When his brothers planned to kill Joseph, Judah persuaded them to sell him instead (Gen 37:26). Genesis 38 tells how he married a Canaanite woman and had three sons, Er, Onan and Shelah. After Er and Onan died, he held Shelah back from their widow Tamar, who later bore Judah twins, Pharez and Zerah. During the famine he pledged himself for Benjamin's safety and became the family's spokesman before Joseph (Gen 43:8). Jacob's blessing promised that the sceptre would not depart from Judah (Gen 49:10). He was…

Joseph (son of Jacob) was the elder of Jacob's two sons by Rachel, named for her hope that the LORD would 'add' another son (Gen 30:24). His envious brothers sold him into Egypt (Acts 7:9), where he served in an Egyptian officer's house and was later imprisoned. Called to interpret Pharaoh's dreams, he was put in charge of Egypt at thirty, received the Egyptian name Zaphnath-paaneah, and married Asenath, who bore Ephraim and Manasseh. During the famine he provided for his father and brothers, who settled in Egypt. He died there at 110 and was embalmed. Moses later carried his bones out of Egypt, and they were buried at Shechem. His name came to stand for the tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh…

Joshua son of Nun, of the tribe of Ephraim (one of the Joseph tribes), was Moses' young assistant and his successor as leader of Israel. He led Israel's fighters against Amalek (Exod 17:9). He and Caleb alone of their generation survived the wilderness (Num 26:65). Moses laid hands on him and charged him to bring Israel into the promised land (Deut 31:7; 34:9). After Moses died, Joshua led the crossing of the Jordan, circumcised the people, and took Jericho, Ai and Hazor. He also made peace with Gibeon and defeated many Canaanite kings. With Eleazar the priest he divided the land among the tribes, giving Hebron to Caleb. In old age he gathered Israel, and the people pledged to serve the…

Paul, also called Saul, was a Jew born in Tarsus who became the leading missionary of the early church. As a young man named Saul he watched the clothes of those who stoned Stephen and then persecuted believers (Acts 7:58). Jesus appeared to him on the road to Damascus, and Ananias restored his sight (Acts 9:17). With Barnabas he preached in Cyprus and Asia Minor, where the people of Lystra called him the god Mercurius (Acts 14:12). Later, with Silas and Timothy, he founded churches in Macedonia and Greece and worked at Ephesus. He was arrested in the Jerusalem temple and heard by Felix, Festus and Agrippa. He appealed to Caesar, survived a shipwreck, and lived two years under guard in Rome…

Simon Peter, also called Cephas and Simeon, was one of the twelve apostles of Jesus and a leading figure in the early church. Son of Jonas and brother of Andrew, he was a fisherman on the Sea of Galilee when Jesus called him (Matt 4:18; John 1:40). With James and John he belonged to an inner group present at the raising of Jairus's daughter and in Gethsemane. He confessed Jesus as the Christ but was sharply rebuked soon after (Mark 8:29; Matt 16:23). During the trials he denied Jesus three times, then wept bitterly. The risen Jesus appeared to him (Luke 24:34; 1 Cor 15:5). In Acts he preached in Jerusalem, healed the sick, was imprisoned by Herod and freed by an angel, and preached to the…

Ephraim was the second son of Joseph and his Egyptian wife Asenath. He was born in Egypt, probably about 1708 BC by inference from context. Joseph named him because God had made him fruitful "in the land of my affliction" (Gen 41:52), and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning "fruitful." According to Gen 48, Jacob adopted Ephraim and his older brother Manasseh as his own sons, crossing his hands to give the younger the greater blessing. Joseph lived to see Ephraim's descendants to the third generation (Gen 50:23). The genealogies name Shuthelah, Becher, Tahan, Ezer, Elead and Beriah among his sons and descendants (Num 26:35; 1 Chr 7:20–23). Most later uses of the name refer to the tribe…

Benjamin (patriarch) was the youngest son of Jacob and the second son of Rachel, making him Joseph's only full brother. Rachel died giving birth to him near Ephrath, about 1739 BC by inference from context. With her last breath she named him Ben-oni, which Smith's Bible Dictionary renders "son of my sorrow." Jacob renamed him Benjamin, meaning "son of the right hand" according to Hitchcock's Bible Names (Gen 35:18). He appears in the account of the brothers' journeys to Egypt, where Joseph gave him a portion five times larger than anyone else's (Gen 43:34). In his final blessing Jacob compared him to a ravening wolf (Gen 49:27). Genealogies name his sons, including Bela, Becher and Ashbel,…

Esau (Edom) was the elder twin son of Isaac and Rebekah and brother of Jacob. He was born red and hairy (Gen 25:25), about 1836 BC by inference from context. He was a hunter and the son Isaac meant to bless, but Jacob received the blessing first (Gen 27:1, 27:30). Genesis 25:30 explains his other name, Edom ("red"), by the red stew for which he sold his birthright. His wives included Adah, Aholibamah and Bashemath, and his sons included Eliphaz, Reuel, Jeush, Jaalam and Korah. Jacob feared him and sent gifts ahead on returning from Haran (Gen 32:19). Esau settled in Seir and became the father of the Edomites (Gen 36:43). His names came to stand for that people. They dealt with Israel at…

Moab was the son of Lot by his older daughter and the ancestor of the Moabites (Gen 19:37). His half-brother Ben-ammi, born to Lot's younger daughter, became the father of the Ammonites. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "of his father." Most later uses of the name refer to his descendants and their land east of the Dead Sea, probably in modern central Jordan. Israel camped in the plains of Moab before crossing the Jordan. There Balak king of Moab summoned Balaam, and there Israel mourned Moses. Eglon of Moab oppressed Israel until Ehud's deliverance, about 1360 BC by inference from context. Ruth's story begins in Moab. David subdued the Moabites, who rebelled after…

Pharaoh (of the Exodus) was the king of Egypt who refused to let the Israelites leave their forced labor. When Moses and Aaron demanded their release, he made the work harder, called on his magicians, and repeatedly agreed and then refused as the plagues struck Egypt. After the death of the firstborn he let the people go, then pursued them with his chariots, and his army was drowned in the Red Sea. Later writers recall these signs and his overthrow (Neh 9:10; Ps 136:15), and Paul quotes God's words to him (Rom 9:17). The Bible never gives his personal name, and "Pharaoh" is also used for other Egyptian kings. Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests Menephtah (Merneptah), son of Rameses II, or…

Jeremiah (also Jeremy or Jeremias) was a prophet of Judah, son of Hilkiah, from a priestly family at Anathoth in Benjamin (Jer 1:1). He prophesied from Josiah's reign, beginning about 628 BC by inference from context, until after the fall of Jerusalem, and he lamented Josiah's death (2 Chr 35:25). The priest Pashur put him in the stocks, and priests sought his death for his temple preaching. His scribe Baruch read his prophecies publicly, and King Jehoiakim ordered both men arrested. Under Zedekiah he was imprisoned and cast into a dungeon, rescued by Ebedmelech the Ethiopian, and held in the prison court until the city fell. Freed by Nebuzaradan, he was later taken to Tahpanhes in Egypt,…

Isaac was the son of Abraham and Sarah, and his name means "laughter" according to Hitchcock's Bible Names. God promised to establish his covenant with Isaac and his descendants (Gen 17:19). Sarah insisted that Ishmael, Hagar's son, should not share Isaac's inheritance (Gen 21:10). At God's command Abraham bound Isaac and laid him on an altar, though the wider account in Gen 22 shows that he was spared (Gen 22:9). He married Rebekah and fathered the twins Esau and Jacob. He lived for a time in Gerar, where his servants dug wells (Gen 26:6, 19), and in old age he blessed his sons (Heb 11:20). He died aged 180 (Gen 35:28), at Mamre according to Gen 35:27. Later scripture often calls God "the…

Samuel was a prophet and the last of Israel's judges, the son of Elkanah and Hannah, of the tribe of Levi (also spelled Shemuel). Hannah named him because she had asked him of the LORD (1 Sam 1:20). As a boy he served under Eli at Shiloh, where the LORD called him by night and revealed himself to him. He later judged Israel at Mizpeh, where the Philistines were routed while he offered sacrifice. In old age he made his sons judges. When the people asked for a king, he anointed Saul, later rebuked him and announced his rejection, and then anointed David. He died at Ramah, mourned by all Israel. Later texts rank him with Moses (Jer 15:1; Ps 99:6). 1 Sam 8:2 names his sons Joel and Abiah, while…

Joab, son of Zeruiah and brother of Abishai and Asahel, was David's nephew (1 Chr 2:16 lists Zeruiah among the sisters of Jesse's sons) and the commander of David's army. He led David's men against Abner's forces at the pool of Gibeon, and he and Abishai later killed Abner to avenge Asahel. He commanded campaigns against Ammon and Syria, and during the Ammonite war he carried out David's plan that led to Uriah's death. He brought Absalom back from Geshur but later killed him during Absalom's revolt. After Absalom made Amasa commander in his place, Joab killed Amasa and put down Sheba's rebellion at Abel of Bethmaachah. He objected to David's census but carried it out. He backed Adonijah's…

Hezekiah was king of Judah, the son of Ahaz and Abijah, who succeeded his father on the throne in Jerusalem (2 Kgs 16:20). Easton's Bible Dictionary dates his 29-year reign to about 726–697 BC. He removed the high places and altars and restored temple worship with offerings and music (2 Chr 29:27; Isa 36:7). In his fourteenth year Sennacherib of Assyria took Judah's fortified cities. Hezekiah paid tribute, stripping gold from the temple doors (2 Kgs 18:13, 16). When the Assyrians later threatened Jerusalem, he prayed for deliverance (2 Kgs 19:15). He fell gravely ill, was told by Isaiah to prepare for death, prayed, and recovered (Isa 38:1; 2 Kgs 20:5). He showed his treasures to envoys…

Manasseh (son of Joseph) was the firstborn of Joseph and his wife Asenath, born in Egypt about 1709 BC by inference from context. Joseph chose the name because God had made him forget his hardship and his father's house (Gen 41:51). When the aged Jacob blessed Joseph's two sons, Joseph placed Manasseh at Jacob's right hand (Gen 48:13). The rest of Gen 48 tells how Jacob crossed his hands and gave the younger Ephraim the greater blessing. According to 1 Chr 7:14, his sons were Ashriel and Machir, and Machir was born to an Aramean concubine. Machir's children were raised on Joseph's knees (Gen 50:23). Manasseh became the ancestor of a tribe of Israel. Half of it settled east of the Jordan in…

Elijah, called Elias in the New Testament, was a prophet from Tishbe in Gilead who confronted King Ahab of Israel, about 910 BC by inference from context. He announced a drought, and a widow at Zarephath fed him from meal and oil that never ran out. He also restored her son to life. On Mount Carmel he challenged the people to choose between the LORD and Baal, and his prayer was answered. The prophets of Baal were killed, and Jezebel's anger drove him to a cave at Horeb. Elisha became his attendant and successor. Elijah later condemned King Ahaziah, called down fire on soldiers sent for him, and parted the Jordan with his mantle before being taken into heaven (2 Kgs 2:11). Malachi foretold…

Absalom was David's third son, born at Hebron to Maacah, daughter of Talmai king of Geshur (2 Sam 3:3; 1 Chr 3:2). He was praised above everyone in Israel for his beauty. After his half-brother Amnon wronged his sister Tamar, Absalom waited two years. He then had his servants kill Amnon at a sheep-shearing feast at Baal-hazor and fled to his grandfather in Geshur. Joab later brought him back to Jerusalem. Absalom gathered chariots and followers, courted people who had grievances, and launched a revolt from Hebron that forced David to flee Jerusalem. Ahithophel advised him, but Hushai, secretly loyal to David, undermined that advice. In the battle that followed, Absalom's head caught in an…

John the Baptist was a prophet who preached in the wilderness of Judea and baptized people in the Jordan, calling for repentance for the forgiveness of sins. He was the son of the priest Zacharias and Elisabeth, and an angel announced his birth and gave his name. Born about 5 BC by inference from context, he lived austerely, and the people widely regarded him as a prophet. He baptized Jesus, said one mightier than he would baptize with the Holy Spirit, and pointed Jesus out as "the Lamb of God." Some of his own disciples, such as Andrew, followed Jesus. After John rebuked Herod for marrying Herodias, his brother Philip's wife, Herod imprisoned him and later had him beheaded. Easton's Bible…

Nebuchadnezzar, also spelled Nebuchadrezzar, was the Chaldean king of Babylon who dominated Judah in its last years. He defeated Pharaoh Necho at Carchemish in Jehoiakim's fourth year and made Jehoiakim his vassal until Jehoiakim rebelled. He carried Jeconiah, the nobles and the craftsmen to Babylon along with the temple vessels, and made Zedekiah king. After Zedekiah also rebelled, he besieged Jerusalem. In his nineteenth year his commander Nebuzaradan destroyed the temple and deported the people, and he put Gedaliah over those who remained. Jeremiah and Ezekiel present him as God's instrument against Judah, Tyre, Egypt and Kedar. In Daniel he has prophetic dreams, sets up a golden image,…

Canaan was a son of Ham and grandson of Noah, listed fourth among Ham's sons after Cush, Mizraim and Put (1 Chr 1:8). After Ham saw his drunken father's nakedness, Noah cursed Canaan, declaring that he would be Shem's servant (Gen 9:18, 26). This entry dates that episode to about 2346 BC, by inference from context. Canaan's firstborn was Sidon, followed by Heth and the ancestors of the Jebusites, Amorites, Girgashites, Hivites, Arkites, Sinites, Arvadites, Zemarites and Hamathites (Gen 10:15–18). Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as the forefather of the Phoenicians and of the peoples west of the Jordan before Israel arrived. His name became the name of their territory, the 'land of…

Jonathan was the eldest son of King Saul and his wife Ahinoam, and the close friend of David. He led a thousand men at Gibeah of Benjamin. With only his armor-bearer he attacked a Philistine garrison and killed about twenty men. Not knowing of Saul's oath forbidding food, he ate honey and was condemned when the lot fell on him, though 1 Sam 14:45 records that the people rescued him. Jonathan made a covenant with David and for a time persuaded Saul not to kill him. He later warned David of Saul's hostility with a signal of arrows and encouraged him while he was in hiding. The Philistines killed him at Gilboa together with his brothers Abinadab and Malchishua. David mourned him in a lament,…

Jeroboam son of Nebat and Zeruah, a widow, was an Ephrathite of Zereda who served Solomon and rebelled against him (1 Kgs 11:26). The prophet Ahijah met him outside Jerusalem, and when Solomon sought to kill him he fled to Shishak of Egypt until Solomon's death. After the northern tribes broke with Rehoboam, they made Jeroboam king over Israel, leaving only Judah to David's house. He became the first king of the northern kingdom, from about 975 BC by inference from context, and reigned twenty-two years. Fearing the people would return to David's line, he set up golden calves at Bethel and Dan and appointed priests from outside the Levites. At the Bethel altar a man of God from Judah…

Ahab was the son of Omri and succeeded him as king of Israel, ruling from Samaria (1 Kgs 16:28). By inference from context his reign began about 918 BC. He married Jezebel, and Kings says he did more evil than all the kings before him (1 Kgs 16:30). The prophet Elijah announced a drought to him and confronted him repeatedly (1 Kgs 17:1; 18:17). Ahab defeated Ben-hadad of Syria and released him under a treaty (1 Kgs 20:34). When Naboth refused to sell his vineyard, Jezebel arranged Naboth's death using Ahab's name. Elijah then pronounced judgment on Ahab's house, and Ahab fasted in sackcloth (1 Kgs 21:8, 20, 27). He allied with Jehoshaphat of Judah against Ramoth-gilead (2 Chr 18:3), where,…

Daniel was a man of Judah taken to Babylon as an exile, where he was trained with Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah and given the Babylonian name Belteshazzar. He refused the king's food and wine and was noted for understanding visions and dreams. He revealed and interpreted Nebuchadnezzar's dream, was made ruler over the province of Babylon and chief of its wise men, and later read the mysterious writing for Belshazzar. Under Darius he was one of three presidents. When he kept praying toward Jerusalem despite a royal decree, he was thrown into a lions' den and came out unhurt. He lived into the reign of Cyrus. The later chapters of his book record his own visions, and Jesus cites "Daniel the…

Reuben was the firstborn son of Jacob and Leah, named by Leah in the hope that her husband would now love her (Gen 29:32). He was born about 1758 BC, by inference from context. He lay with Bilhah, his father's concubine (Gen 35:22). Jacob's dying words address him as firstborn, and the following verse links his loss of preeminence to that act (Gen 49:3–4). When his brothers plotted against Joseph, Reuben persuaded them not to kill him and tore his clothes on finding the pit empty (Gen 37:21, 29). Later he offered his own two sons as a pledge for Benjamin's safe return from Egypt (Gen 42:37). His four sons, Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron and Carmi, went down with him to Egypt (Gen 46:9). His…

Jehoshaphat (Josaphat in Matt 1:8) was king of Judah, the son of Asa and Azubah, who succeeded his father in the fourth year of Ahab of Israel. His reign began about 914 BC, by inference from context. He first strengthened Judah against Israel but later made peace and allied with Ahab, joining him in battle at Ramoth-gilead, where he asked that a prophet of the LORD be consulted. He also joined Jehoram of Israel and the king of Edom against Moab, and Elisha agreed to speak out of regard for him. Chronicles records his wealth, tribute from Philistines and Arabians, his appointment of judges in Jerusalem, and a victory over a great invading army after prayer at the temple. A shipping venture…

Levi (patriarch) was the third son of Jacob and Leah. Leah named him in the hope that her husband would now be "joined" to her (Gen 29:34). With his brother Simeon, he avenged the rape of their sister Dinah by killing the men of Shechem, as Gen 34 relates. Jacob rebuked them for it at the time (Gen 34:30) and again in his final words (Gen 49:5). Levi went down to Egypt with Jacob. His sons were Gershon, Kohath and Merari (1 Chr 6:16). His daughter Jochebed, born in Egypt, became the mother of Aaron, Moses and Miriam (Num 26:59). Easton's Bible Dictionary notes from Exod 6:16 that he died in Egypt aged 137. His birth is placed about 1756 BC, by inference from context. His descendants formed…

Dan was a son of Jacob and the first of two sons born to him by Bilhah, Rachel's servant. Naphtali was his full brother, and Easton's Bible Dictionary counts Dan as Jacob's fifth son. Rachel named him, saying that God had judged her and heard her voice, and the name is usually taken to mean "judge" (Gen 30:6). His birth is placed at about 1755 BC, by inference from context. Only one son, Hushim, is recorded for him (Gen 46:23). In Jacob's final blessing he is pictured as a serpent by the road that bites a horse's heels (Gen 49:17). He was the ancestor of the tribe of Dan. Most later uses of the name refer to that tribe or to the northern city of Laish, which the Danites renamed after him…

Pharaoh (of Joseph) was the unnamed king of Egypt during Joseph's years there. His officer Potiphar bought Joseph as a slave (Gen 39:1). In anger he jailed his chief butler and chief baker, whose dreams Joseph interpreted (Gen 41:10). When Pharaoh dreamed of seven thin ears of grain devouring seven full ones, the butler remembered Joseph. Joseph explained that seven years of plenty would be followed by seven years of famine. Pharaoh set Joseph over Egypt and gave him his ring, the name Zaphnathpaaneah and a wife, Asenath (Gen 41:42–45). He later welcomed Joseph's family, sent wagons for Jacob, let them settle in Goshen, and was blessed by Jacob (Gen 47:7). Through Joseph he acquired the…

Eleazar was the third son of Aaron and Elisheba, and the brother of Nadab, Abihu and Ithamar. He married a daughter of Putiel, who bore him Phinehas. With his father and brothers he was consecrated as a priest. After Nadab and Abihu died childless, he and Ithamar carried on the priestly service, and he was made chief over the Levites who kept the sanctuary. When Aaron was about to die, Aaron's garments were put on Eleazar, and he succeeded him as priest. He stood with Moses at the census, at Joshua's commissioning, and over the Midianite spoils. Later he and Joshua divided Canaan among the tribes at Shiloh. He was buried in the hill country of Ephraim on land belonging to Phinehas. In…

Balaam, son of Beor, was a soothsayer from Pethor in Mesopotamia, probably on the Euphrates. Balak son of Zippor, king of Moab, sent for him to curse the Israelites camped near his land. God at first forbade him to go, then allowed it on condition that he speak only what he was told. On the way his donkey turned aside from the angel of the LORD, and Balaam, after striking her, had his eyes opened to see the angel. At altars Balak built, including on the top of Peor, he blessed Israel three times instead of cursing them, and the two parted. Num 31:16 blames his counsel for Israel's sin at Peor and the plague that followed, and Israel later killed him with the sword. Later writers recall him…

Gad was the seventh son of Jacob and the first son of Zilpah, Leah's servant, making him the full brother of Asher. He was born in Paddan-aram, about 1753 BC by inference from context. Leah named him, and the King James Version explains the name as "a troop," while Easton's Bible Dictionary prefers "fortune" (Gen 30:11). Little is recorded about Gad himself. He went down to Egypt with Jacob's family along with seven sons, whose names appear in slightly different forms in Gen 46:16 and Num 26:15. Jacob's deathbed blessing plays on his name, saying a troop would attack him but he would overcome in the end. He was the ancestor of the tribe of Gad, a herding tribe that settled in Gilead east of…

Satan, a Hebrew word meaning "adversary" or "accuser" (Easton's Bible Dictionary), is the Bible's name for a spiritual opponent of God and of people. In Job he comes before the LORD among the sons of God and, with permission, afflicts Job (Job 1:6–12; 2:7). He provokes David to number Israel (1 Chr 21:1) and stands beside Joshua the high priest to resist him (Zech 3:1–2). In the Gospels he tempts Jesus in the wilderness, and Jesus' opponents call him Beelzebub, prince of the devils, a name Jesus treats as Satan's (Matt 12:24–26). He is said to enter Judas and to fill Ananias's heart to lie (John 13:27; Acts 5:3). Paul describes him hindering, tempting and disguising himself as an angel of…

Pontius Pilate was the Roman governor of Judaea under the emperor Tiberius (Luke 3:1). Easton's Bible Dictionary dates his governorship to about AD 26–36. Luke 13:1 reports that he killed Galileans while they were offering sacrifices. When the Jewish council handed Jesus over to him, about AD 30 by inference from context, Pilate questioned him about being King of the Jews and said repeatedly that he found no fault in him. He sent Jesus to Herod, and the two rulers became friends that day. The crowd kept pressing him and warned that releasing Jesus would make him no friend of Caesar. Pilate then washed his hands in public, had Jesus scourged, and sentenced him to be crucified. He wrote the…

Abner, son of Ner, was commander of King Saul's army. 1 Sam 14:50–51 can be read to call him Saul's uncle or, since Ner and Saul's father Kish were both sons of Abiel, Saul's cousin. This entry follows the cousin reading, as does the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. Abner brought David before Saul after Goliath was killed, sat beside the king at meals, and was rebuked by David for failing to guard Saul. After Saul died, he made Saul's son Ishbosheth king at Mahanaim. When David's men defeated his forces at Gibeon, he killed Joab's brother Asahel. Later he quarrelled with Ishbosheth over one of Saul's concubines (Rizpah, named in 2 Sam 3:7) and met David at Hebron, offering to…

Asa was the third king of Judah after the division of the kingdom, the son of Abijah (Abijam) and the father of Jehoshaphat. He also appears in the genealogy of Jesus (Matt 1:7–8). He became king in the twentieth year of Jeroboam of Israel and reigned 41 years, roughly 956–914 BC by inference from context. He destroyed idols, renewed the altar of the LORD, and removed Maachah from her position as queen mother, burning her idol at the brook Kidron, though the high places remained. He defeated an Ethiopian army at Mareshah. When Baasha of Israel fortified Ramah, Asa paid Benhadad of Syria with temple and palace treasure to intervene, then used Ramah's stones and timber to build Geba and…

Elisha, son of Shaphat of Abel-meholah, was a prophet in the northern kingdom of Israel and the successor of Elijah. God told Elijah to anoint him, and Elijah found him plowing and cast his mantle on him. He served Elijah, who "poured water on the hands of Elijah," and asked for a double portion of his spirit before Elijah was taken up. He then parted the Jordan with Elijah's mantle and was recognized by the sons of the prophets as their leader. His recorded deeds include healing Jericho's waters, multiplying a widow's oil, restoring the Shunammite woman's son to life, curing Naaman the Syrian of leprosy, and foretelling the end of the famine in besieged Samaria. He advised kings, told…

Isaiah, son of Amoz, was a prophet in Judah whose visions concerned Judah and Jerusalem during the reigns of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah (Isa 1:1). This entry dates his prophecies to about 759 BC, by inference from context. He brought his son Shear-jashub to meet King Ahaz (Isa 7:3). He also had a second son, Maher-shalal-hash-baz, and he walked naked and barefoot for three years as a sign against Egypt and Ethiopia (Isa 20:3). When the Assyrian king Sennacherib threatened Jerusalem, Isaiah told Hezekiah not to be afraid (2 Kgs 19:6, 20). Later he announced Hezekiah's coming death, prescribed a lump of figs for his recovery, and gave the sign of the shadow turning back (2 Kgs…

Job was a man of the land of Uz, described as blameless and upright, one who feared God and avoided evil. He regularly offered sacrifices on behalf of his children. When Satan asked whether Job served God for nothing, Job lost his livestock, servants and children and was then struck with painful sores, yet the text says he did not sin or blame God. Three friends, Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar, came to comfort him, and a long series of speeches followed in which Job defended his innocence. A younger man, Elihu, then rebuked Job and the friends. The LORD answered Job and afterward said that Job, not his friends, had spoken rightly. Job prayed for them, and his wealth was restored twice over. His…

Baal, meaning "lord" or "master" (Hitchcock's Bible Names), was the chief male god of the Canaanites and Phoenicians, often worshipped alongside Ashtaroth (Judg 2:13). At Peor in Moab, Israel joined in the worship of Baal-peor, and those involved were put to death (Num 25:3–5; Deut 4:3). Gideon tore down his father's altar to Baal and was renamed Jerubbaal (Judg 6:25–32). King Ahab served Baal after marrying Jezebel, daughter of the Sidonian king Ethbaal. Elijah then challenged 450 prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel (1 Kgs 16:31; 18:19–26). Jehu destroyed Baal's temple in Samaria, and a house of Baal in Jerusalem was torn down when Athaliah fell (2 Kgs 10:19–27; 11:18). Jeremiah condemns the…

Zedekiah, originally named Mattaniah, was the last king of Judah. A son of Josiah and Hamutal, he was placed on the throne by Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon in place of his nephew Jehoiachin (Coniah), and Nebuchadnezzar renamed him. He began reigning at twenty-one, about 597 BC by inference from context, and ruled eleven years in Jerusalem. The prophet Jeremiah urged him to submit to Babylon. Zedekiah consulted him repeatedly, sometimes in secret, yet also kept him confined. Zedekiah rebelled against Babylon, and Jerusalem was besieged until his eleventh year, when the city was broken into. He fled by night but was captured in the plains of Jericho and brought to Riblah. There his sons were…

Mordecai was a Jew of the tribe of Benjamin, the son of Jair, who lived at Shushan (Susa), the Persian royal city, during the reign of Ahasuerus (Xerxes). He raised his orphaned cousin Esther as his own daughter and continued to guide her after she became queen. While sitting in the king's gate, he exposed a plot by two chamberlains to kill the king. He refused to bow to Haman, and this led Haman to plan the destruction of all the Jews. Mordecai mourned in public and urged Esther to intervene. Haman was then hanged on the gallows he had built for Mordecai. The king gave Mordecai his signet ring, and Mordecai became second only to the king. He sent letters establishing the feast of Purim.…

Gideon, also called Jerubbaal, was a judge of Israel and son of Joash the Abiezrite of Ophrah. While he was threshing wheat in a winepress to hide it from the Midianites, an angel of the LORD called him to deliver Israel, and he built an altar there named Jehovahshalom. He tore down Baal's altar by night, rallied his clan, and asked for a sign with a fleece. God reduced his army to three hundred men, who routed Midian with trumpets and broken pitchers. He then pursued and killed the kings Zebah and Zalmunna. He turned down Israel's offer to make his family hereditary rulers (Judg 8:23), but made a gold ephod at Ophrah that became a snare. The land then had forty years of peace, starting…

Josiah was a king of Judah, the son of Amon and Jedidah. The people made him king at eight years old after his father was assassinated, and he reigned thirty-one years in Jerusalem, about 640–609 BC by inference from context. He removed the high places at Bethel and in Samaria, burning bones on the Bethel altar as a man of God had foretold by name in 1 Kgs 13:2. He also put away mediums and idols to carry out the book of the law that Hilkiah the priest found in the temple. In his eighteenth year he held a Passover unmatched since Samuel's day. Jeremiah and Zephaniah prophesied during his reign. He went out against Pharaoh Necho at Megiddo, was shot by archers, and died, and all Judah…

Naphtali was a son of Jacob and the second son born to him by Bilhah, Rachel's servant, making him the full brother of Dan. Rachel named him to mark her 'great wrestlings' with her sister Leah (Gen 30:8). Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning as 'that struggles or fights.' He went down to Egypt with his four sons, Jahzeel, Guni, Jezer and Shillem (Gen 46:24; 1 Chr 7:13). Jacob's blessing calls him 'a hind let loose' who 'gives goodly words' (Gen 49:21). Little else is told of him personally. Most later mentions concern the tribe descended from him. It settled in the north, west of the upper Jordan and the Sea of Galilee, with Kedesh among its cities (Josh 19:32; Josh 21:32). Assyria…

Sarah, first called Sarai, was the wife of Abraham and the mother of Isaac. Gen 20:12 calls her Abraham's half-sister, a daughter of Terah by a different mother. She was barren and went with Abraham from Haran into Canaan. Twice, in Egypt and at Gerar, Abraham called her his sister, and she was taken into a ruler's household before being given back. After ten years in Canaan without children, she gave her Egyptian maid Hagar to Abraham, and Hagar bore Ishmael. Conflict between the two women followed. God renamed her Sarah and promised she would have a son. Overhearing the promise in her old age, she laughed. At about ninety she bore Isaac, and she later had Hagar and Ishmael sent away. She…

Jehu was a king of Israel, the son of Jehoshaphat and grandson of Nimshi; several other people in the Bible share the name. God told Elijah to anoint him king (1 Kgs 19:16–17). While Jehu was an army commander at Ramoth-gilead, a messenger from Elisha anointed him, and his fellow officers proclaimed him king. He drove furiously to Jezreel, shot King Joram with an arrow, and had Ahaziah of Judah struck down. According to Easton's Bible Dictionary, he then had Jezebel thrown from a window. He killed the rest of Ahab's house and, by staging a great sacrifice to Baal, gathered Baal's worshippers and had them killed. He still kept the golden calves at Bethel and Dan. He reigned 28 years in…

Noah was the son of Lamech, who named him with the hope that he would bring comfort from the toil of the cursed ground (Gen 5:29). Described as a just man who walked with God, he found favor with the LORD when the earth was filled with violence (Gen 6:8–13). He built the ark as commanded and entered it with his wife, his sons Shem, Ham and Japheth, and their wives, eight people in all, when the flood came in his six hundredth year (Gen 7:6–13; 1 Pet 3:20). Afterwards he built an altar and offered sacrifices, and God blessed him and made a covenant with all flesh (Gen 8:20; 9:1, 17). He later became drunk, and his son's conduct led to a curse on Canaan (Gen 9:24). He lived 350 years after…

Esther, also called Hadassah, was a Jewish woman who became queen of the Persian king Ahasuerus. Orphaned as a girl, she was raised in Shushan by her cousin Mordecai, the son of her father Abihail's brother, who took her as his own daughter (Esth 2:7). Gathered among the maidens brought to the palace, she was chosen by the king and crowned in Vashti's place, while keeping her people and family hidden at Mordecai's instruction (Esth 2:17; 2:20). When Haman obtained a decree to destroy the Jews, Mordecai urged her to plead with the king. She approached him uninvited, was received with the golden sceptre, and invited him and Haman to two banquets. At the second she asked for her life and her…

Laban was the son of Bethuel and brother of Rebekah. He lived at Haran in Padanaram and is called "the Syrian," that is, the Aramean. Gen 29:5 calls him "son of Nahor," meaning descendant, since Bethuel was Nahor's son. With Bethuel he agreed to Rebekah's marriage to Isaac. Years later Rebekah's son Jacob fled to him. Laban promised Jacob his younger daughter Rachel in return for his service but gave him Leah first, saying local custom required the elder to marry first. He then gave Rachel too, with the maids Zilpah and Bilhah. He urged Jacob to stay, saying the LORD had blessed him for Jacob's sake, and they agreed on wages from the flocks. When Jacob left secretly, Laban pursued him to…

Zebulun was the tenth son of Jacob and the sixth and last son born to Leah. At his birth Leah said that now her husband would dwell with her, and the name is usually taken to mean "dwelling" or "habitation" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Nothing is recorded of his personal life beyond his three sons, Sered, Elon and Jahleel, who went down with Jacob to Egypt and became the founders of the tribe's clans. Jacob's blessing foresaw Zebulun living by the sea, with his border reaching toward Sidon. His descendants formed the Tribe of Zebulun, which received land in Galilee and fought alongside Naphtali under Barak against Sisera. The New Testament uses the Greek form Zabulon, and Matthew places…

Haman, son of Hammedatha the Agagite, was the chief official of the Persian king Ahasuerus, who placed him above all the other princes (Esth 3:1). When Mordecai the Jew refused to bow to him, Haman resolved to destroy all the Jews in the empire. He cast Pur, the lot, to set a date, promised silver to the royal treasury, and sealed a decree with the king's ring. Queen Esther invited him with the king to two banquets. Between them he was made to lead Mordecai through the city in honour. At the second banquet Esther named him as the enemy, and he was hanged on the gallows he had built for Mordecai. His wife was Zeresh, and his ten sons were later killed and hanged. Easton's and Smith's Bible…

Rachel (spelled Rahel in Jer 31:15) was the younger daughter of Laban and the wife Jacob loved most. Jacob met her as she came with her father's sheep. He served Laban seven years for her but was first given her elder sister Leah, and then received Rachel as well. Long childless, she envied Leah and gave Jacob her maid Bilhah, whose sons Dan and Naphtali she named. God then opened her womb and she bore Joseph. When Jacob left Laban, Rachel stole her father's household images and hid them by sitting on them. She died giving birth to Benjamin on the way to Ephrath (Bethlehem), about 1739 BC by inference from context, and Jacob set a pillar on her grave. Ruth 4:11 names her with Leah as…

Jesse was the father of King David, a man of the tribe of Judah living at Bethlehem, and the son of Obed, grandson of Boaz and Ruth. When God sent Samuel to anoint a king from among his sons, Jesse presented the older sons first and had not called the youngest, David, who was tending the sheep. He later sent David to Saul with bread, wine and a young goat, and sent food to his three eldest sons, Eliab, Abinadab and Shammah, serving in Saul's army. 1 Sam 17:12 says he had eight sons, while 1 Chr 2:13–15 names seven. David is often called "the son of Jesse," sometimes dismissively by opponents. Isaiah speaks of a "root of Jesse," a passage Paul quotes, and Jesse appears in the genealogies of…

Asher was the eighth son of Jacob and the second son of Zilpah, Leah's servant, making Gad his full brother. He was born in Paddan-aram, about 1752 BC by inference from context. Leah named him, saying "Happy am I," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "happiness." As one of Joseph's brothers, he would have shared in the events of Joseph's sale and the later journeys to Egypt during the famine. He went down to Egypt with his children Imnah, Ishvah, Ishvi and Beriah and his daughter Serah (Gen 46:17; 1 Chr 7:30). Jacob's blessing promised Asher rich food, and Moses' blessing spoke of him dipping his foot in oil. He was the ancestor of the tribe of Asher, which settled along…

Rehoboam was the son and successor of Solomon; his mother was Naamah, an Ammonite. He became king at forty-one and reigned seventeen years in Jerusalem, about 975–958 BC by inference from context. At Shechem, where Israel gathered to make him king, Jeroboam and the people asked for relief from Solomon's burdens. Rehoboam rejected the advice of his father's older counsellors. After his tribute officer Adoram was stoned to death, he fled to Jerusalem, and only Judah, with Benjamin, stayed loyal. His attempt to retake the north was halted by a message through the prophet Shemaiah. He fortified cities in Judah. In his fifth year Shishak of Egypt came against Jerusalem, and Rehoboam made bronze…

Balak, son of Zippor, was king of Moab when Israel camped near his territory after defeating the Amorites. Alarmed, he sent elders of Moab and Midian with payment to summon the prophet Balaam from Aram to curse Israel. When Balaam refused, Balak sent more distinguished princes and promised him honour. He met Balaam at a city on the Arnon border and took him to the high places of Baal, then to other vantage points including the top of Peor, building altars and offering bulls and rams at each. Each time Balaam blessed Israel instead, and Balak angrily complained that he had blessed them three times. The two then parted. Later books recall the episode: Josh 24:9 says he warred against Israel,…

Simeon was the second son of Jacob and Leah, named because Leah said the LORD had heard that she was unloved (Gen 29:33). Several other people in the Bible share the name. With his brother Levi he avenged their sister Dinah by killing the men of Shechem, which alarmed Jacob (Gen 34:25, 30), and Jacob's dying words condemn the pair's violence (Gen 49:5). When the brothers went to Egypt for grain during the famine, Joseph kept Simeon bound as a hostage until they returned with Benjamin (Gen 42:24, 36; 43:23). His sons included Jemuel (Nemuel), Jamin, Ohad, Jachin, Zohar (called Zerah in Chronicles) and Shaul, whose mother was a Canaanite (Gen 46:10; 1 Chr 4:24). He was the ancestor of the…

Zadok, son of Ahitub, was a Levite priest descended from Aaron's son Eleazar who served as one of the two chief priests under King David, alongside Abiathar. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies him with the valiant young Zadok who joined David at Hebron (1 Chr 12:28). During Absalom's revolt he and the Levites carried the ark out of Jerusalem, but David sent them back, and Zadok's son Ahimaaz carried news to the king. When Adonijah claimed the throne, Zadok stayed loyal and, at David's order, anointed Solomon king at Gihon with oil from the tabernacle. Solomon then put him in Abiathar's place. Chronicles also places him before the tabernacle at Gibeon. His descendants, 'the house of…

Ahasuerus was the Persian king of the Book of Esther, who reigned from Shushan over 127 provinces stretching from India to Ethiopia (Esth 1:1–2). He removed his queen Vashti from her position when she refused his summons during a feast (Esth 1:15–19), and in his seventh year he took Esther as queen (Esth 2:16). He promoted Haman, who sent out a decree in the king's name to destroy the Jews (Esth 3:1; 3:12). After Esther intervened, Ahasuerus gave Haman's house to her and made Mordecai second only to himself (Esth 8:1; 10:3). Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries identify him as probably Xerxes I, who reigned about 486–465 BC. The name also appears in Ezra 4:6 and in Dan 9:1, where…

Issachar was the ninth son of Jacob and the fifth borne to him by Leah. Leah named him after her words "God hath given me my hire," so the name is linked to "hire" or "reward" (Gen 30:18). His birth is placed at about 1752 BC by inference from context, probably in Paddan-aram, as Easton's Bible Dictionary notes. Little is recorded of him personally beyond the shared story of Jacob's sons, including the family's move to Egypt. He had four sons: Tola, Puah (Phuvah), Jashub (called Job in Gen 46:13) and Shimron. Jacob's deathbed blessing pictured him as a strong donkey lying down between two burdens. He was the ancestor of the tribe of Issachar. The tribe numbered 54,400 fighting men at Sinai…

Merari was the third son of Levi, listed with his brothers Gershon and Kohath, and one of Jacob's family who went down to Egypt (Gen 46:11; Exod 6:16). Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "bitter." His sons Mahli and Mushi founded the two Merarite families (Exod 6:19; Num 3:33). 1 Chr 24:26–27 also names Jaaziah, apparently as a further son, though the wording is unclear. In the wilderness the Merarites camped north of the tabernacle under Zuriel. They were responsible for its boards, bars, pillars and sockets, served under Ithamar the priest, and were given four wagons and eight oxen to carry them (Num 3:35–36; 7:8). Under Joshua they received twelve cities from…

Midian was a son of Abraham by Keturah, one of six brothers, and the father of Ephah, Epher, Hanoch (or Henoch), Abida and Eldaah (Gen 25:2–4; 1 Chr 1:32–33). His name is also used for the people descended from him, the Midianites, and for their land. Moses fled to the land of Midian and married into the family of Jethro, the priest of Midian. Later the elders of Midian joined Moab in hiring Balaam. After the affair at Peor, Israel fought the Midianites and killed five of their kings. In the time of the judges Midian oppressed Israel for seven years until Gideon defeated them, about 1258 BC by inference from context. Later prophets recall "the day of Midian" as a great deliverance. Smith's…

Samson was a judge of Israel, the son of Manoah, known for his great strength and his lone fights against the Philistines, who ruled Israel in his day (Judg 15:11). Against his parents' wishes he married a Philistine woman of Timnath. At the wedding feast he posed a riddle, his wife coaxed the answer from him, and she was later given to his companion. In revenge he tied firebrands to foxes' tails and loosed them among Philistine crops. After the Philistines burned his wife and her father, he killed a thousand men with the jawbone of an ass. At Gaza he carried off the city gates. Delilah repeatedly tried to learn the secret of his strength and finally betrayed him. Captured and blinded, he…

Ahaz was king of Judah, the son and successor of Jotham. He became king at twenty and reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem, beginning about 742 BC by inference from context, and the text says he did not do right as David had. When Rezin of Syria and Pekah of Israel besieged Jerusalem, Isaiah met him, but Ahaz declined to ask for a sign. Instead he sent temple and palace silver and gold to Tiglath-pileser of Assyria for help. After meeting Tiglath-pileser in Damascus, he had the priest Urijah copy an altar he saw there and rearranged the temple furnishings. According to Chronicles, he also broke up the temple vessels and shut its doors. A sundial bore his name. He was buried in Jerusalem but…

Jehoiakim, originally named Eliakim, was a king of Judah and the son of Josiah and Zebudah. After Pharaoh Necho of Egypt removed his brother Jehoahaz, Necho made Eliakim king and renamed him Jehoiakim. He taxed the land to pay Egypt's demands. He became king at twenty-five and reigned eleven years in Jerusalem, roughly 609–598 BC by inference. During his reign Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon defeated Egypt at Carchemish and besieged Jerusalem, carrying off temple vessels. Jehoiakim served Babylon for three years and then rebelled. He had the prophet Urijah brought back from Egypt and killed. He also burned the scroll of Jeremiah's prophecies, which Baruch then rewrote. Jeremiah foretold that no…

Abimelech, one of several men of this name in the Bible, was a son of Gideon (also called Jerubbaal) by a concubine from Shechem. Backed by his mother's relatives, he won over the men of Shechem, used seventy pieces of silver from the house of Baal-berith to hire followers, and killed his seventy brothers "upon one stone." Only Jotham escaped (Judg 9:5). The Shechemites then made him king, about 1218 BC by inference from context. Jotham warned that Abimelech and Shechem would destroy each other. After three years Shechem turned against him under Gaal son of Ebed. Abimelech defeated Gaal, destroyed Shechem and sowed it with salt, and burned about a thousand people in its tower. While…

John the Apostle was a son of Zebedee and brother of James, a Galilean fisherman and partner of Simon Peter, whom Jesus called while he was mending nets with his father. He was one of the twelve apostles, and Jesus surnamed the brothers Boanerges, "sons of thunder." With Peter and James he formed an inner group present at the raising of Jairus's daughter, the Transfiguration and Gethsemane. The Gospels record him forbidding an outsider to cast out demons, offering to call down fire on a Samaritan village, and seeking honor with James. After the ascension he appears with Peter healing a lame man, standing trial before the council, and visiting Samaria. Paul calls him a "pillar" (Gal 2:9).…

Amaziah was a king of Judah, the son and successor of Joash and the father of Uzziah, also called Azariah. His mother was Jehoaddan of Jerusalem. He became king at twenty-five after his father was murdered. He reigned twenty-nine years in Jerusalem, roughly 839–810 BC by inference from context. He mustered Judah's army and hired Israelite troops for a hundred talents. At a man of God's word he sent them home, and the dismissed soldiers raided cities of Judah. He defeated the Edomites in the Valley of Salt, but then set up and worshipped Edom's gods, and a prophet rebuked him. He challenged Jehoash king of Israel, was defeated and captured at Beth-shemesh, and part of Jerusalem's wall was…

Lot was the son of Haran and the nephew of Abraham (Abram). He left Ur of the Chaldees with his grandfather Terah, then went with Abram into Canaan and returned with him from Egypt. Their flocks grew so large that their herdsmen quarreled, and Abram proposed they part. Lot chose the well-watered plain of the Jordan and settled toward Sodom, later living in the city. When invading kings raided Sodom he was carried off, and Abram rescued him. Later two angels came to Sodom, and Lot took them into his house. When the men of the city attacked his door, the angels pulled him inside. They then hurried him, his wife and two daughters out before the cities were destroyed. Jesus later recalled Lot's…

Sihon was king of the Amorites, ruling from his city of Heshbon east of the Jordan. He had earlier taken land from the king of Moab as far as the Arnon River, a conquest celebrated in a poem quoted in Num 21:27–29. His territory ran from Aroer on the Arnon to the Jabbok River, the border of Ammon, and included the Jordan valley up to the Sea of Galilee. When Israel asked permission to pass peacefully through his land, Sihon refused. He gathered his army and fought them at Jahaz, where Israel defeated him and took his cities. Moses then gave his kingdom, together with that of Og king of Bashan, to Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh. Later writers, including Joshua, Nehemiah and the Psalms,…

Uzziah, also called Azariah (and Ozias in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus), was king of Judah, the son of Amaziah and Jecoliah of Jerusalem. The people made him king at sixteen, and he reigned fifty-two years in Jerusalem, roughly 810–758 BC by inference from context. Chronicles describes a strong ruler who received gifts from the Ammonites, built fortified towers in Jerusalem and equipped a large organized army. When he entered the temple to burn incense, the priests opposed him. While he was angry with them, leprosy broke out on his forehead. He lived in a separate house until his death while his son Jotham governed, and he was buried in a field belonging to the royal burial ground. Jotham's…

Asaph (Levite) was a son of Berechiah from the tribe of Levi and one of the chief musicians in David's time. When the ark was brought to Jerusalem, the Levites appointed him with Heman and Ethan to sound bronze cymbals. He then led the musicians who served before the ark every day, and David handed a psalm of thanksgiving to him and his fellow Levites. His sons Zaccur, Joseph, Nethaniah and Asarelah (elsewhere Jesharelah) led groups of singers under his direction. Later passages call him a seer and name him alongside David as a leader of song. The 'sons of Asaph' served as temple singers through Hezekiah's reforms and after the return from exile. Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests they may…

Leah was the elder daughter of Laban and sister of Rachel. She is described as "tender eyed," in contrast to her beautiful sister. Jacob served Laban for Rachel, but Laban gave him Leah on the wedding night instead. Jacob then married Rachel as well and loved her more. Leah bore Jacob six sons, Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar and Zebulun, and a daughter, Dinah. She named several of them in the hope of winning her husband's love. Zilpah, the maid Laban gave her, bore Gad and Asher, whom Leah named. Leah agreed with Rachel to leave Laban's house with Jacob. She was buried in the family tomb with Abraham, Sarah, Isaac and Rebekah, which Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies as the cave of…

Caleb son of Jephunneh, called a Kenezite, represented the tribe of Judah among the men Moses sent to explore Canaan. When the others discouraged the people, he urged them to go up and take the land at once, and with Joshua son of Nun he tore his clothes in protest. Because he 'wholly followed the LORD,' he and Joshua were the only adults of that generation allowed to enter the land. He was later named to help divide it. At Gilgal he reminded Joshua of Moses' promise and received Hebron, driving out the three sons of Anak. He offered his daughter Achsah to whoever captured Kirjath-sepher. Othniel son of Kenaz, called Caleb's younger brother, took it and married her, and Caleb gave her upper…

Eli was the priest at the sanctuary in Shiloh before Israel had kings, and the father of the priests Hophni and Phinehas (1 Sam 1:3, 9). He first mistook Hannah's silent prayer for drunkenness, then blessed her. He later received her son Samuel, who served under him and whom he taught to answer the Lord's call (1 Sam 1:13–17; 3:8–9). When he was very old and nearly blind, he heard of his sons' misconduct. A man of God, and then Samuel, announced judgment on his house (1 Sam 2:22, 27; 3:12–14). The ark was captured in battle with the Philistines and his sons were killed. The ninety-eight-year-old Eli heard the news by the wayside, and according to 1 Sam 4:18 he fell, broke his neck and died,…

Nun was the father of Joshua, Moses' assistant and successor as leader of Israel. He is known almost entirely through the repeated phrase "Joshua the son of Nun," which appears throughout Exodus, Numbers, Deuteronomy and Joshua, and later in 1 Kgs 16:34 and Neh 8:17, where the son's name is spelled Jeshua. Num 13:8 places the family in the tribe of Ephraim, one of the two tribes descended from Joseph. The genealogy of Ephraim in 1 Chr 7:27 spells his name Non and names his father as Elishama, with Joshua (Jehoshua) as his son. Beyond this, as Easton's Bible Dictionary notes, nothing more is known of him. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "fish," and the International…

Abiathar was a priest, the son of Ahimelech son of Ahitub, and the only one of his father's house to escape when Saul had the priests killed. He fled to David carrying the ephod, which David used through him to seek guidance (1 Sam 23:9; 30:7). Under David he served as priest alongside Zadok, helped bring up the ark, and is named among the king's counselors. During Absalom's revolt he stayed in Jerusalem with the ark, and his son Jonathan carried news to David. He later backed Adonijah's bid for the throne. Solomon spared his life for his past service but banished him to Anathoth and put Zadok in his place, fulfilling the word against Eli's house. His son Ahimelech also served as priest.…

Barnabas was the name the apostles gave to Joses, a Levite from Cyprus. Acts 4:36 explains it as “son of consolation.” An early member of the Jerusalem church, he brought the newly converted Saul to the apostles and vouched for him. Sent by Jerusalem to Antioch, he fetched Saul from Tarsus, carried famine relief to Jerusalem with him, and was listed among Antioch’s prophets and teachers. Set apart with Saul, he went on the first missionary journey (about AD 45, by inference) through Cyprus and Asia Minor. At Lystra the crowd called him Jupiter, and Acts calls him an apostle. He took part in the Jerusalem council, though Paul writes that he was once drawn into other Jews’ insincerity (Gal…

Kohath was the second of the three sons of Levi, listed among Jacob's family who went down to Egypt (Gen 46:11). He had four sons, Amram, Izhar, Hebron and Uzziel, and lived 133 years (Exod 6:18). Exod 6:20 says Amram married Jochebed, Kohath's sister, which makes Kohath the grandfather of Moses and Aaron. His descendants, the Kohathites, formed one of the three main divisions of the Levites. In the wilderness they camped on the south side of the tabernacle. After Aaron's sons had covered its most holy objects, the Kohathites carried them on their shoulders, without touching them. Korah, who led a rebellion with Dathan and Abiram, was his grandson through Izhar. Under Joshua the remaining…

Nathan was a prophet at the courts of David and Solomon. When David proposed building a house for the ark, Nathan first approved, then brought him a message from the LORD that he received that night (2 Sam 7:2–17). After David's sin with Bathsheba, Nathan confronted him with a parable about a rich man and a poor man, telling him, "You are the man." He later delivered the name Jedidiah for Solomon. When Adonijah claimed the throne, Nathan alerted Bathsheba and David, then joined Zadok the priest in anointing Solomon king at Gihon. Chronicles cites a book of Nathan for the acts of David and Solomon, and links him with David's orders for the Levite musicians. Jewish tradition credits him and…

Rebekah was the daughter of Bethuel, granddaughter of Abraham's brother Nahor, and sister of Laban of Padan-aram (Gen 22:23; 25:20). Abraham's servant met her drawing water at a well, and she agreed to go with him to marry Isaac, who loved her and was comforted after his mother's death. The marriage is placed about 1856 BC, by inference from context. She was barren until Isaac prayed for her, and she then bore the twins Esau and Jacob. Isaac favored Esau, but Rebekah loved Jacob. Among the Philistines, Isaac called her his sister because he feared men would kill him for her beauty. When she overheard Isaac promising Esau a blessing, she dressed Jacob in Esau's clothes to obtain it. She…

Zerubbabel was a descendant of David's royal line who led the first group of Jewish exiles from Babylon back to Jerusalem and directed the rebuilding of the temple. He is usually called the son of Shealtiel, though 1 Chr 3:19 names Pedaiah as his father. Easton's Bible Dictionary explains that "son" here means grandson or nephew. With Jeshua the high priest, he rebuilt the altar and began the temple work. He refused help from the peoples whom Esarhaddon had settled in the land. In the second year of Darius, the prophets Haggai and Zechariah addressed him as governor of Judah and urged him to finish the house. Haggai called him God's chosen signet. Matthew lists him among the ancestors of…

Adam was the first man in the Genesis account, formed by God and placed in the garden of Eden. His name is the ordinary Hebrew word for 'man,' which Hitchcock's Bible Names glosses as 'earthy' or 'red.' He named the animals, and God made a woman from one of his ribs. Adam called her Eve. After both ate from the forbidden tree, they hid from God, who cursed the ground for Adam's sake and clothed them in skins. Adam fathered Cain, Abel and Seth, the last at age 130, as well as other sons and daughters, and he died at 930. The genealogies in 1 Chr 1:1 and Luke 3:38 begin with him. Paul contrasts Adam, in whom all die, with Christ as 'the last Adam' (1 Cor 15:22, 45). The date of about 4004 BC…

Ahaziah was king of Judah for one year, the son of King Jehoram and Athaliah, and the youngest son of his father. He is also called Jehoahaz and Azariah. After raiders killed his older brothers, the people of Jerusalem made him king. His age at accession is given as 22 in 2 Kgs 8:26 and as 42 in 2 Chr 22:2. While visiting his wounded uncle Joram, king of Israel, at Jezreel, he rode out with him to meet Jehu and was caught up in Jehu's revolt against the house of Ahab. Kings says he was struck near Ibleam and died at Megiddo. Chronicles says he was found hiding in Samaria and killed. His death was about 886 BC, by inference from context. Athaliah then destroyed the royal family, but his…

Baasha son of Ahijah, of the tribe of Issachar, was the third king of the northern kingdom of Israel and, as Easton's Bible Dictionary notes, founder of its second dynasty. While Nadab son of Jeroboam was besieging the Philistine town of Gibbethon, Baasha conspired against him, killed him, and took the throne in the third year of Asa king of Judah. He reigned twenty-four years from Tirzah, beginning about 953 BC by inference from context. He was at war with Asa throughout and fortified Ramah to cut off movement into Judah. He abandoned the work when Asa paid the king of Syria to break his alliance with Israel. The prophet Jehu son of Hanani announced that Baasha's house would end like…

Gedaliah was the son of Ahikam and grandson of Shaphan, appointed by Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon to govern the people left in Judah after Jerusalem fell. He was one of several men of this name in the Bible. Based at Mizpah, he received Jeremiah, who had been released from prison into his care. He promised the Judean army captains and their men that it would go well with them if they settled in the land and served Babylon. Jews scattered in Moab, Ammon and Edom then returned to him and gathered a large harvest. Johanan son of Kareah warned him that Ishmael son of Nethaniah had been sent by Baalis king of the Ammonites to kill him, but Gedaliah did not believe it. In the seventh month…

Jehoiada, one of several men of this name, was the priest in Jerusalem (the high priest, in Easton's Bible Dictionary) who restored David's line after Queen Athaliah seized Judah's throne. His wife Jehoshabeath, King Jehoram's daughter, hid the infant Joash from Athaliah's massacre. In the seventh year Jehoiada bound the captains and guards by oath in the temple, armed them with King David's weapons, crowned and anointed Joash, and had Athaliah killed outside the temple. He made a covenant binding king and people to the LORD and reorganized the temple services. Joash did right while Jehoiada instructed him, and together they repaired the temple, using a collection chest for funds. Jehoiada…

Jephthah was a Gileadite warrior and judge of Israel, called a mighty man of valour and the son of Gilead by a harlot. His half-brothers drove him from the family inheritance, and he lived in the land of Tob with a band of followers. When the Ammonites attacked Israel, the elders of Gilead brought him back and made him their head and captain at Mizpeh. His messages to the Ammonite king failed. The Spirit of the LORD then came on him, and he vowed to offer whatever first came out of his house if he won. He defeated Ammon, and his only child, a daughter, came out to meet him. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes Judg 11:39 to mean she was sacrificed, while some interpreters hold she was devoted to…

Korah (Levite) was a son of Izhar, grandson of Kohath and great-grandson of Levi. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that Izhar was a brother of Amram, which made Korah a cousin of Moses and Aaron. With the Reubenites Dathan, Abiram and On, he led a revolt in the wilderness against Moses and Aaron. Moses told Korah and his company to bring censers with incense before the LORD so that God would show whom he had chosen. The earth opened and swallowed the rebels' households and Korah's men, and fire consumed 250 men. Their censers became a reminder that only Aaron's descendants could offer incense. Korah's sons did not die. Their descendants, the Korahites, later served as gatekeepers of the…

Gershon, also called Gershom in several passages of Chronicles, was a son of Levi and the brother of Kohath and Merari. He is always listed first among Levi's sons, and Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries take him to be the eldest. He went down to Egypt with Jacob's family. His sons are named as Libni and Shimei. 1 Chr 23:7 names them Laadan and Shimei, so Laadan is probably another name for Libni. Num 26:59 names Jochebed as a daughter of Levi, which makes her Gershon's sister. His descendants, the Gershonites, formed one of the three main Levite families. In the wilderness they carried the tabernacle's tent, coverings and door hangings under the oversight of Ithamar, using two wagons…

Nebat was the father of Jeroboam, the first king of the northern kingdom of Israel after it broke away from the house of David. He is known only through the phrase "Jeroboam the son of Nebat," which appears again and again in Kings and Chronicles. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the phrase served to distinguish this Jeroboam from the later Jeroboam son of Joash. Nebat is identified as an Ephrathite, meaning an Ephraimite, from Zereda. His wife was Zeruah, who is described as a widow at the time Jeroboam rebelled against Solomon (1 Kgs 11:26). By inference, Nebat had died by then. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name is usually explained as meaning "sight" or…

Zeruiah was the sister of David and the mother of Joab, Abishai and Asahel, three leading commanders of David's army (1 Chr 2:16). Her sister was Abigail, mother of Amasa. 2 Sam 17:25 calls Abigail a daughter of Nahash, while Chronicles counts both women as sisters of Jesse's sons. This entry therefore treats Zeruiah as David's half-sister, probably through a shared mother. Her husband is never named, and her sons are almost always identified by her name: "Joab the son of Zeruiah" and "Abishai the son of Zeruiah." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests this may reflect her husband's early death or her own prominence. That work also notes that, by inference from 2 Sam 2:32,…

Abishai was a son of Zeruiah and brother of Joab and Asahel. 1 Chr 2:16 places Zeruiah among David's sisters, making him David's nephew. He volunteered to go with David by night into Saul's camp and urged him to kill the sleeping king, but David refused. With Joab he pursued Abner after Asahel's death and later joined in killing him. He led troops against the Ammonites, and 1 Chr 18:12 credits him with killing eighteen thousand Edomites in the Valley of Salt. During Absalom's revolt he twice asked to kill Shimei for cursing David, and he commanded a third of David's army in the decisive battle. He pursued the rebel Sheba and rescued David by killing a Philistine giant, named Ishbi-benob in…

Adonijah was the fourth son of David, born to Haggith at Hebron (2 Sam 3:4; 1 Chr 3:2). When David was old, Adonijah declared, "I will be king," gathered chariots, horsemen and fifty runners, and won the support of Joab and the priest Abiathar. Zadok, Benaiah, Nathan and David's mighty men did not join him. He held a sacrificial feast by the stone of Zoheleth near En-rogel, where guests hailed him as king. Nathan and Bathsheba reminded David of his oath that Solomon would reign, and Solomon was made king. Adonijah's guests scattered, and he grasped the horns of the altar, asking Solomon to swear to spare him. Later, through Bathsheba, he asked to marry Abishag the Shunammite. Solomon…

Boaz (Greek form Booz) was a wealthy landowner of Bethlehem in the tribe of Judah and a relative of Elimelech, the late husband of Naomi. When Naomi's widowed Moabite daughter-in-law Ruth gleaned in his field, he welcomed her, praised her loyalty to Naomi, shared his reapers' meal with her and told his workers to let her glean freely through the barley and wheat harvests. After Ruth came to him at night on the threshing floor, Boaz went to the town gate, where a nearer kinsman gave up his right to redeem the family land. Before the elders, Boaz bought Elimelech's property and married Ruth, an arrangement Easton's Bible Dictionary links to the levirate law. Their son Obed was the grandfather…

Jonah, son of Amittai, was a prophet of Israel from Gath-hepher, called Jonas in the New Testament. According to 2 Kgs 14:25, he foretold that Jeroboam II would restore Israel's borders, which places him in or shortly before that king's reign. This entry dates his prophecies to about 825 BC, by inference from context. The book bearing his name tells how God sent him to Nineveh, but he fled by ship from Joppa toward Tarshish. When a storm arose, the sailors cast lots, and the lot fell on him. They threw him overboard, and a great fish swallowed him. He prayed from inside it for three days and nights until it cast him onto dry land. Sent again, he warned that Nineveh would be overthrown in…

Manasseh (son of Hezekiah), also called Manasses, was a king of Judah who succeeded his father Hezekiah at age twelve and reigned fifty-five years in Jerusalem. His mother was Hephzibah. By inference from context, he reigned from about 697 to 642 BC. Kings describes him leading Judah into idolatry worse than that of the nations driven out before Israel, building altars in the two courts of the temple, and shedding much innocent blood. Later passages blame his sins for Judah's eventual exile. Chronicles adds that Assyrian commanders took him in fetters to Babylon, where he prayed and was restored to his kingdom, acknowledging the LORD as God. He was buried in the garden of his own house, the…

Timotheus, the King James form of Timothy, was a disciple from the Lystra and Derbe area who became one of Paul's closest companions. His mother, Eunice, was a believing Jewish woman and his father was a Greek (Acts 16:1). He joined Paul and Silas on the second missionary journey and stayed behind at Berea before rejoining Paul at Athens and then Corinth (Acts 17:14–15; 18:5). Paul sent him on errands to Thessalonica, Macedonia, Corinth and Philippi, and he travelled with Paul into Asia (1 Thess 3:2, 6; Acts 19:22; 20:4). He is named as co-sender of several of Paul's letters, and Paul calls him his "son in the faith" (1 Tim 1:2), a phrase usually taken to mean Paul had converted him. Two…

Abimelech (King of Gerar) was a Philistine ruler of Gerar who dealt with both Abraham and Isaac. After Abraham called Sarah his sister, Abimelech took her, but God warned him in a dream that she was a married woman. He had not touched her. He rebuked Abraham, returned Sarah with gifts of livestock and servants, and invited him to settle in his land. God then healed his household of barrenness (Gen 20:17–18). Later, with his army commander Phichol, he made a covenant with Abraham at Beersheba after a dispute over a well. In Isaac's time Abimelech discovered that Rebekah was Isaac's wife, not his sister, and ordered that no one harm them. He later asked Isaac to leave and then came to make…

Benaiah son of Jehoiada was one of David's leading warriors and later commander of Solomon's army. Several other men in the Bible share his name. He came from Kabzeel. His recorded feats include killing two champion warriors of Moab and a lion in a pit on a snowy day, which made him famous among David's mighty men (2 Sam 23:20–22). David put him over the Cherethites and Pelethites, the royal bodyguard. He also commanded the army division that served in the third month, with his son Ammizabad in his division. 1 Chr 27:5 calls either him or his father a chief priest; Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries apply the title to Jehoiada. Benaiah did not side with Adonijah, and he helped bring…

Herod Antipas was a son of Herod the Great, by Malthace according to Easton's Bible Dictionary, and ruled Galilee as tetrarch during the ministry of Jesus (Luke 3:1). He married Herodias, the wife of his brother Philip. When John the Baptist told him the marriage was unlawful, Herod imprisoned him, although he respected John and listened to him gladly. At his birthday feast the daughter of Herodias danced before his guests, and Herod promised her whatever she asked. This led to John's beheading. By inference from context, the imprisonment was about AD 27 and the execution about AD 29. Hearing of Jesus' works, Herod wondered whether John had risen from the dead. Some Pharisees warned Jesus…

Hiram, called Huram in Chronicles, was king of Tyre in the days of David and Solomon. He sent David messengers, cedar timber, carpenters and masons to build him a house (2 Sam 5:11; 1 Chr 14:1). Described as always a friend of David, he made a league with Solomon. He supplied cedar and fir for the temple, and his builders worked alongside Solomon's, in return for yearly wheat and oil. Solomon later gave him twenty cities in Galilee. They did not please him, yet he sent Solomon 120 talents of gold, and Chronicles speaks of these cities as restored to Solomon. His experienced sailors joined Solomon's fleets to Ophir and Tarshish, bringing back gold, almug wood, precious stones and ivory. This…

Joash, also called Jehoash, was a king of the northern kingdom of Israel. He was the son of Jehoahaz and grandson of Jehu, and is distinct from several others of the same name, including his contemporary Joash king of Judah.
