He succeeded his father in Samaria in the thirty-seventh year of Joash of Judah and reigned sixteen years, roughly 840–825 BC by inference from context. When the prophet Elisha lay dying, Joash visited him and wept over him. He defeated Ben-hadad son of Hazael of Syria three times and recovered Israelite cities lost under his father. When Amaziah king of Judah challenged him, Joash answered with a fable of a thistle and a cedar. He then captured Amaziah at Beth-shemesh,…

Judas Iscariot was one of the twelve apostles of Jesus and the one who betrayed him. John calls him the son of Simon (John 6:71), and Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries explain his surname as "man of Kerioth," a town in Judah. The Gospels distinguish him from another apostle named Judas, the brother of James (Luke 6:16; John 14:22). He kept the group's money bag. He went to the chief priests to arrange the betrayal, and at the last supper Jesus identified him by handing him dipped bread. He led an armed crowd to a place where Jesus often met his disciples and singled Jesus out with a kiss. When Jesus was condemned, Judas regretted it and returned the thirty pieces of silver. Matt 27:5…

Nehemiah, son of Hachaliah and brother of Hanani, was a Jew living in Persia who became governor (Tirshatha) of Judah and is the narrator of the book that bears his name. His account opens at Shushan, the Persian royal residence, in the twentieth year of the king (Neh 1:1). Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies the king as Artaxerxes Longimanus and describes Nehemiah as the royal cupbearer, who obtained leave to go to Jerusalem and rebuild its walls, probably about 446 BC. As governor he stood with Ezra the priest and scribe when the law was read, telling the weeping people that the day was holy and not for mourning (Neh 8:9). He was the first to seal the covenant (Neh 10:1). Later passages…

Shaphan son of Azaliah, grandson of Meshullam, was the scribe, or royal secretary, of King Josiah of Judah. In Josiah's eighteenth year the king sent him to the temple about the money collected for its repair. There the high priest Hilkiah gave him the newly found book of the law. Shaphan read it, reported to the king and read it aloud to him (2 Kgs 22:8–10). He was then one of the group sent to consult the prophetess Huldah. His family remained prominent. His son Ahikam protected Jeremiah, his son Elasah carried Jeremiah's letter to Babylon, and Baruch read Jeremiah's scroll in the chamber of his son Gemariah. His grandson Gedaliah was made governor of Judah by Nebuchadnezzar and was later…

Amalek was a son of Eliphaz, Esau's eldest son, by his concubine Timna, making him a grandson of Esau and his wife Adah (Gen 36:12). He is listed among the chiefs ("dukes") of Edom descended from Eliphaz (Gen 36:16). The list in 1 Chr 1:36 places Timna among Eliphaz's sons alongside Amalek. His name also stands for the people descended from him, the Amalekites. As a people, Amalek attacked Israel at Rephidim after the exodus and was defeated by Joshua while Moses held up his hands (Exod 17:8–13). The LORD then declared lasting war against Amalek (Exod 17:14–16; Deut 25:17–19). Amalek later joined Moab against Israel (Judg 3:13). Saul struck Amalek and captured its king Agag (1 Sam 15:2–20),…

Ezra was a priest and scribe of the tribe of Levi who led a company of Jewish exiles from Babylon to Jerusalem in the reign of Artaxerxes king of Persia, about 459 BC according to Easton's Bible Dictionary. His genealogy calls him the son of Seraiah. Easton's suggests he may have been a grandson, and 1 Chr 6:14–15 makes Seraiah the father of Jehozadak (Josedech). Described as "a ready scribe in the law of Moses," Ezra received a royal letter letting him draw on the treasuries and appoint judges beyond the river. In Jerusalem he mourned the people's marriages to foreign wives and led an oath and an inquiry into the matter. Later, with Nehemiah the governor, he read the law aloud from a…

Og was the Amorite king of Bashan, the region east of the Jordan, who reigned from Ashtaroth and Edrei. He is described as the last survivor of the remnant of the giants, the Rephaim. His iron bedstead, nine cubits long and four wide (about 13 by 6 feet), was said to be kept at Rabbah of the Ammonites. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that some take it to be a basalt sarcophagus. Soon after Israel defeated Sihon, Og led his people out to fight them at Edrei and was defeated and killed. Israel took his sixty cities in the region of Argob, and Moses gave his kingdom to Reuben, Gad and the half tribe of Manasseh, mainly the Machirites. Rahab, the Gibeonites, Nehemiah and the…

Uriah the Hittite was a soldier in King David's army, one of David's elite warriors known as the mighty men, and the husband of Bathsheba, daughter of Eliam. While Uriah was away fighting the Ammonites, David took Bathsheba. David then called Uriah back to Jerusalem and urged him to go home, but Uriah slept at the palace door, saying he would not enjoy his house while the ark, Israel and his comrades were camped in the field. David sent him back with a letter telling Joab to put him where the fighting was fiercest and then pull back, and Uriah was killed by archers on the city wall. By inference from the surrounding chapters, the city was probably Rabbah, the Ammonite capital. The prophet…

Amnon was David's firstborn son, born in Hebron to Ahinoam of Jezreel (2 Sam 3:2; 1 Chr 3:1). He became so infatuated with Tamar, the sister of his half-brother Absalom, that he made himself ill over her. His cousin Jonadab, son of David's brother Shimeah, advised him to pretend to be sick. Amnon then asked David to send Tamar to prepare food for him. When she came, he sent everyone out, forced her, and then turned on her with intense hatred and drove her away. Absalom said nothing to Amnon but hated him for what he had done. According to 2 Sam 13:23, two years later Absalom invited the king's sons to a sheep-shearing feast. There he had his servants kill Amnon once he was merry with wine.…

Baruch son of Neriah, son of Maaseiah, was the scribe and companion of the prophet Jeremiah. During the Babylonian siege, Jeremiah handed him the deeds for the field bought from his cousin Hanameel and told him to keep them safe. In the fourth year of King Jehoiakim, Baruch wrote Jeremiah's prophecies on a scroll as the prophet dictated them. Because Jeremiah was barred from the temple, Baruch read the scroll there, then read it again to the royal officials, who told him and Jeremiah to hide. After the king burned the scroll, Baruch wrote a new, expanded copy. After Jerusalem fell, Jewish leaders accused him of turning Jeremiah against them, and he was taken with the remnant that went to…

Hazael was a king of Syria (Aram), ruling from Damascus, in the time of Elisha. God told Elijah to anoint him king over Syria (1 Kgs 19:15), though the anointing itself is not recorded. Hazael first appears as an officer of King Ben-hadad, sent with forty camels' load of gifts to ask Elisha whether the sick king would recover. Elisha wept and foretold both the harm Hazael would do to Israel and his rise to the throne. The next day Ben-hadad was smothered with a wet cloth, and Hazael reigned in his place. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes Hazael himself to be the killer. He fought Joram of Israel at Ramoth-gilead, struck Israel throughout its territory, and oppressed it for all of Jehoahaz's…

Ishmael son of Nethaniah, grandson of Elishama and of the royal line, was one of the army captains who came to Gedaliah at Mizpah after the king of Babylon made Gedaliah governor. He is not the son of Abraham who bears the same name. Johanan son of Kareah warned Gedaliah that Baalis king of the Ammonites had sent Ishmael to kill him, but Gedaliah refused to believe it. In the seventh month Ishmael and ten men ate with Gedaliah at Mizpah, then killed him along with the Jews and Chaldean soldiers there. He then killed a group of arriving men and threw their bodies into the pit King Asa had made, sparing ten who offered hidden stores of food. He carried off the remaining people, including the…

Jehoiachin, also called Jeconiah, Coniah and (in Matthew) Jechonias, was a king of Judah, the son of Jehoiakim and of Nehushta, daughter of Elnathan of Jerusalem. He succeeded his father and reigned in Jerusalem for only three months. 2 Kgs 24:8 gives his age at accession as eighteen, while 2 Chr 36:9 says eight and adds ten days to the reign. He surrendered to Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon and was taken into exile with his mother, wives, officials, nobles and craftsmen, about 598 BC by inference from context. Nebuchadnezzar put Zedekiah, a son of Josiah, on the throne in his place. Jeremiah declared that Coniah and his descendants would be cast out, though another prophet foretold his return.…

Jehoiada was the father of Benaiah, who commanded David's Cherethites and Pelethites and later became Solomon's army commander (2 Sam 8:18; 1 Kgs 2:35). He is known almost entirely through his son's title, "Benaiah the son of Jehoiada." 2 Sam 23:20 calls Benaiah "the son of a valiant man, of Kabzeel," which may describe Jehoiada as a brave man from Kabzeel in southern Judah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that some read the phrase as describing Benaiah himself. 1 Chr 27:5 can be read as calling Jehoiada a chief priest. This entry also includes the Jehoiada of 1 Chr 12:27, leader of the Aaronites who joined David with 3,700 men, and treats him as probably the same man.…

Joshua, also called Jeshua, was the son of Josedech (Jozadak) and the high priest of the Jews who returned from exile in Babylon with Zerubbabel. He is one of several people in the Bible with this name. With Zerubbabel, the governor of Judah, he rebuilt the altar at Jerusalem and began work on the temple. They also refused to let outsiders take part in the building, as King Cyrus had commanded. The prophet Haggai addressed him by name and urged him to be strong and finish the work. In Zechariah's visions he stands before the angel of the LORD in filthy garments, with Satan opposing him, and he is later crowned with crowns of silver and gold. He was the father of Joiakim, who in turn began a…

Mary (Mother of Jesus) was the wife of Joseph and the mother of Jesus. While she was engaged to Joseph, a descendant of David, an angel told her she would bear a son, and she accepted, calling herself "the handmaid of the Lord" (Luke 1:38). Matthew and Luke say she conceived by the Holy Spirit before she and Joseph came together. She stayed with her relative Elisabeth for about three months, then travelled with Joseph to Bethlehem, where Jesus was born. She was present when the wise men came and at his presentation in the temple. The Gospels name James, Joses, Simon and Jude as Jesus' brothers, and traditions differ on whether they were Mary's own sons. She stood at the cross and later…

Abijah, also called Abijam and Abia, was king of Judah, the son and successor of Rehoboam and the father of Asa. His mother was Maachah, called the daughter of Absalom (2 Chr 11:20). 2 Chr 13:2 names her Michaiah, daughter of Uriel of Gibeah. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes Michaiah as a variant of the name and 'daughter' as meaning granddaughter. Rehoboam made him chief among his brothers, intending him to be king. He began to reign in Jeroboam's eighteenth year and ruled three years in Jerusalem, about 958–956 BC by inference from context. Chronicles describes his war with Jeroboam of Israel. Achish was a Philistine king of Gath, called son of Maoch (1 Sam 27:2) or Maachah (1 Kgs 2:39). Maharai the Netophathite was one of David's mighty men, the elite warriors listed in 2 Sam 23:28 and 1 Chr 11:30. His title links him to Netophah, a town near Bethlehem in Judah. Mahli was a Levite of the clan of Merari, the son of Mushi and grandson of Merari, the son of Levi (1 Chr 6:47). Memucan was one of the seven princes of Persia and Media at the court of King Ahasuerus. These men "saw the king's face" and held the highest rank in the kingdom (Esth 1:14). When Queen Vashti refused the king's summons to appear at his feast, Ahasuerus asked these counsellors what should be done.…

Meshullam son of Berechiah and grandson of Meshezabeel was one of the men who repaired the wall of Jerusalem under Nehemiah. He is listed working on a section next to Meremoth son of Urijah (Neh 3:4), and later as repairing the stretch opposite his own chamber (Neh 3:30). He is generally taken to…

Michah was a Levite of the family of Uzziel, a branch of the Kohathite clan. In the lists of Levites arranged in King David's time, he is named as the first, or chief, of the sons of Uzziel, with Jesiah (also spelled Isshiah) second (1 Chr 23:20; 24:25). His son Shamir is named after him (1 Chr…

Mikloth was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, listed in the genealogy of the family of Saul as a son of the founder of Gibeon and his wife Maachah (Easton's Bible Dictionary). Chronicles names that father Jehiel, or Jeiel. This entry follows the view that he is the same man as Abiel, whom 1 Sam 9:1…

Milcom was the national god of the Ammonites, called in 1 Kgs 11:5 "the abomination of the Ammonites." Solomon, influenced by his foreign wives, worshipped Milcom along with Ashtoreth of the Sidonians and Chemosh of Moab, and this is given as a reason the kingdom would be divided after him (1 Kgs…

Miniamin was a priest, or the head of a priestly family, in the period after the return from Babylon. Under the spelling Miamin he is listed among the priests who came back with Zerubbabel (Neh 12:5), and Easton's Bible Dictionary calls him a chief priest. A Mijamin appears among the priests who…

Mizzah was a son of Reuel and a grandson of Esau through Esau's wife Bashemath. He is listed as the youngest of Reuel's four sons, with his brothers Nahath, Zerah and Shammah (Gen 36:13; 1 Chr 1:37). Moadiah was a priest, or a priestly family named after him, in the period after the return from exile. Nehemiah lists Maadiah among the priests who came back from Babylon with Zerubbabel (Neh 12:5). In the next generation, in the days of the high priest Joiakim, Piltai was head of the priestly…

n: Mother of the Wife of Simon
bio: The Mother of the Wife of Simon was the mother-in-law of Simon Peter, the apostle. The three Gospels that tell her story all say she lay sick with a fever in Simon's house, which Luke calls "a great fever" (Luke 4:38). Mark and Luke place this immediately after Jesus left the synagogue, and Mark's…

Naamah was a wife of King Solomon and the mother of Rehoboam, his successor as king of Judah. Each of the three verses that mention her names her as Rehoboam's mother and calls her an Ammonite, a formula repeated in the official summaries of his reign in 1 Kgs 14:21, 31 and 2 Chr 12:13. She was…

Nahash was king of the Ammonites in the time of Saul. He besieged Jabesh-gilead, east of the Jordan. When its men offered to make a treaty and serve him, he agreed only on condition that he gouge out every man's right eye, as a disgrace on all Israel (1 Sam 11:1–2). According to the rest of the…

Nahash was a king of the Ammonites and the father of Hanun, who succeeded him on the throne. He had shown kindness to David at some point, and when Nahash died, David sent servants to Hanun to comfort him over his father's death (2 Sam 10:2; 1 Chr 19:1–2). The text does not say what that kindness…

Nahath was a son of Reuel and a grandson of Esau through Esau's wife Bashemath. His brothers were Zerah, Shammah and Mizzah. He is listed first among Reuel's sons, and Smith's Bible Dictionary takes him to be the eldest. Genesis 36 names him as one of the "dukes", or clan chiefs, who came from…

Nahath was a Levite of the clan of Kohath and an ancestor of the prophet Samuel. His name appears in different forms in the genealogies: Tohu in 1 Sam 1:1, Toah in 1 Chr 6:34, and Nahath in 1 Chr 6:26. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries both describe him as a Kohathite Levite, and the…

Nepheg was one of the sons of King David born in Jerusalem, after David had moved his capital there from Hebron. He appears only in the three lists of those sons, each time between Elishua or Nogah and Japhia (2 Sam 5:15; 1 Chr 3:7; 14:6). His mother is not named, and the text records nothing about…

Obadiah, also called Abda, was a Levite descended from Jeduthun through Galal who lived in Jerusalem after the return from exile in Babylon. In 1 Chr 9:16 he is called Obadiah son of Shemaiah. The parallel list in Neh 11:17 names him Abda son of Shammua, and the International Standard Bible…

Omar was a son of Eliphaz, the firstborn son of Esau, which made him a grandson of Esau. He is named second among Eliphaz's sons, after Teman, in the genealogy of Esau's descendants in Gen 36:11, and again in the parallel list in 1 Chr 1:36. His brothers included Zepho, Gatam and Kenaz, and the…

On, son of Peleth, was a man of the tribe of Reuben who joined Korah, Dathan and Abiram when they gathered men to challenge the leadership of Moses and Aaron during the wilderness period (Num 16:1). His name appears only in this opening verse. As Smith's Bible Dictionary notes, he is not mentioned…

Parosh was the ancestor and head of an Israelite family that returned to Jerusalem from exile in Babylon. The lists of returnees in Ezra 2:3 and Nehemiah 7:8 count 2,172 of his descendants, the largest lay family in those lists. Seven men from this family appear in Ezra 10:25 among those who had…

Pekahiah was a king of Israel, the son and successor of Menahem. He began to reign in Samaria in the fiftieth year of Azariah (Uzziah) king of Judah and ruled for two years. His other acts were recorded in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel. The surrounding passage adds that he…

Phichol was the chief captain, or army commander, of Abimelech, the Philistine king of Gerar. He went with Abimelech to Abraham, who acknowledged that God was with Abraham, and was present when the two made a covenant at Beersheba, after which they returned to the land of the Philistines (Gen…

Philip was a son of Herod the Great and the first husband of Herodias. He is mentioned only in connection with the imprisonment of John the Baptist. His brother Herod Antipas, the tetrarch, married Herodias, and John rebuked him for it. That rebuke led Herod to have John bound and put in prison…

Phut, also spelled Put, was the third of the four sons of Ham listed in the Table of Nations, after Cush and Mizraim and before Canaan (Gen 10:6; 1 Chr 1:8). Through Ham he was a grandson of Noah. Unlike his brothers, he is given no listed descendants. Elsewhere the name stands for a people or land…

Poti-pherah was an Egyptian priest of On, the city later known as Heliopolis, near modern Cairo. His daughter Asenath was given to Joseph as his wife by Pharaoh when Pharaoh raised Joseph to authority over Egypt and gave him the Egyptian name Zaphnathpaaneah (Gen 41:45). Through Asenath,…

Puah was the second-listed of the four sons of Issachar and a grandson of Jacob. His brothers were Tola, Jashub and Shimron. Genesis 46:13 names him Phuvah among the family members who went down to Egypt with Jacob, and Numbers 26:23 spells his name Pua and calls him the ancestor of the Punites,…

Rimmon was a man of Beeroth, a town counted as part of the tribe of Benjamin, and the father of Baanah and Rechab. His sons were captains of raiding bands serving Ish-bosheth, Saul's son. Serah was the daughter of Asher and a granddaughter of Jacob. Shammah was a son of Reuel and a grandson of Esau through Esau's wife Bashemath. He is named third among Reuel's four sons, after Nahath and Zerah and before Mizzah (Gen 36:13; 1 Chr 1:37). In the list of Edom's chiefs he appears as "duke Shammah," one of the clan leaders descended from Reuel in…

Shammua was a son of King David, born in Jerusalem after David made the city his capital. He is listed first among the sons born there, ahead of Shobab, Nathan and Solomon (2 Sam 5:14; 1 Chr 14:4). In 1 Chr 3:5 he is called Shimea, and that verse names all four as sons of Bathshua daughter of…

Shebaniah was a Levite in the time of Ezra and Nehemiah, one of several men of that name in the Bible. Shelomith was a Levite in King David's reign, descended from Moses' son Eliezer through a line of descendants: Rehabiah, Jeshaiah, Joram, Zichri and then Shelomith, whose father was Zichri (1 Chr 26:25). Shemaiah was a Levite, the firstborn of the sons of Obed-edom, listed among the gatekeepers in David's reign (1 Chr 26:4). His younger brothers included Jehozabad, Joah, Sacar, Nethaneel, Ammiel, Issachar and Peulthai. His sons were Othni, Rephael, Obed, Elzabad, Elihu and Semachiah. They are…

Shemiramoth was a Levite musician in David's time. He was one of the Levites of the second rank appointed to accompany the ark of the covenant when it was brought up to Jerusalem (1 Chr 15:18). Shephatiah was the ancestor of a family whose descendants returned from exile in Babylon to Jerusalem and Judah. Sheshai was one of the three sons of Anak, named with his brothers Ahiman and Talmai, who lived at Hebron when Moses sent spies into Canaan (Num 13:22). The Anakim were remembered as people of great size, which is why some reference works call Sheshai a giant. Joshua 15:14 says Caleb drove the…

Sheshan was a man of the tribe of Judah, the son of Ishi and a descendant of Appaim in the Jerahmeelite clan of the genealogy in 1 Chronicles 2. The text says he had no sons, only daughters, and that he gave one of his daughters as wife to his Egyptian servant Jarha. She bore Attai, through whom…

Shillem was the fourth-named son of Naphtali, one of the sons of Jacob, and so a grandson of Jacob through Bilhah, Rachel's servant. Shimron was the fourth son of Issachar, son of Jacob, and the founder of the Shimronite clan in the tribe of Issachar. His brothers were Tola, Puah and Jashub. Shuah was a Canaanite man whose daughter became the wife of Judah, son of Jacob. According to Gen 38:2, Judah met her while staying near Hirah the Adullamite, married her, and had children with her. 1 Chr 2:3 names their three sons as Er, Onan and Shelah and spells the father's name Shua. His…

Shubael, also called Shebuel, was a Levite descended from Moses through Moses' son Gershom. He is named as the chief of the sons of Gershom (1 Chr 23:16) and appears among the descendants of Amram, Moses' father, with a son or descendant named Jehdeiah (1 Chr 24:20). He is described as "ruler of…

Shupham was a son of Benjamin and the founder of a Benjamite clan, the Shuphamites, listed in the census of Num 26:39. His name appears in several forms. Genesis 46:21 calls him Muppim and counts him among the sons of Benjamin who went down to Egypt with Jacob. In 1 Chr 8:5 he appears as…

Shuthelah was a son of Ephraim and the head of the Shuthalhite family within the tribe of Ephraim (Num 26:35). Stephanas was a Christian of Corinth whose household was the first in the Roman province of Achaia to accept the gospel. Paul calls it the "firstfruits of Achaia" and says it had devoted itself to serving fellow believers. His household was one of the few Paul baptized personally at Corinth.…

Talmai was one of the three sons, or descendants, of Anak, along with Ahiman and Sheshai. They lived at Hebron when the Israelite spies passed through the hill country of Canaan (Num 13:22). The Anakim were known as men of great size, a reputation reflected in the spies' report in the surrounding…

Talmai, son of Ammihud, was king of Geshur in the time of David. Geshur was a small kingdom, described by the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia as Aramean, which probably lay east of the Jordan near the Sea of Galilee. Talmai's daughter Maacah became one of David's wives, and she was the…

Teman was a son of Eliphaz and a grandson of Esau. He heads the list of Eliphaz's sons in both genealogies, alongside Omar, Zepho (Zephi in 1 Chr 1:36), Gatam and Kenaz. Trophimus was a Christian from Ephesus, in the Roman province of Asia, who traveled with Paul. He was one of the companions who went with Paul from Greece through Macedonia into Asia near the end of his third missionary journey (Acts 20:4). He went on with Paul to Jerusalem. There, people who had…

Urijah, also spelled Uriah, was a priest of the period after the return from exile in Babylon. He is known only as the father of Meremoth and the son of Koz. Urijah, son of Shemaiah of Kirjath-jearim, was a prophet in Judah during the reign of King Jehoiakim. He prophesied in the name of the LORD against Jerusalem and the land of Judah, delivering a message that matched Jeremiah's. When Jehoiakim, his officers and the princes heard his words, the king…

Wife of Simon was the wife of the apostle Simon Peter. She is never named, and she appears only indirectly: the Gospels mention her when Jesus came to Simon's house and found her mother lying sick with a fever (Matt 8:14; Mark 1:30; Luke 4:38). Zacchaeus was a rich chief tax collector at Jericho whom Jesus met while passing through the town on his way to Jerusalem, about AD 30 by inference from context (Luke 19:2). Zaccur was a Levite, the first-named of the sons of Asaph, David's chief musician. He and his brothers Joseph, Nethaniah and Asarelah (called Jesharelah in 1 Chr 25:14) served under their father's direction and "prophesied" with music by the king's order (1 Chr 25:2). When David's musicians were…

Zachariah was a king of the northern kingdom of Israel and the son of Jeroboam (Jeroboam II), whom he succeeded on the throne (2 Kgs 14:29). He began to reign in Samaria in the thirty-eighth year of Azariah king of Judah, and he ruled for only six months (2 Kgs 15:8). The surrounding verses (2 Kgs…

Zacharias, also called Zechariah, was the son of Jehoiada the priest and lived in the reign of King Joash of Judah. After Jehoiada's death, the Spirit of God came on him. He stood above the people and warned that because they had forsaken the LORD, the LORD had forsaken them (2 Chr 24:20). The next…

Zattu was the ancestor of a large Israelite lay family that returned from exile in Babylon to Judah with Zerubbabel. Ezra's list gives the descendants of Zattu as 945 (Ezra 2:8). Nehemiah's parallel list gives 845 (Neh 7:13), probably a copying difference between the two lists. In Ezra's later…

Zeeb was one of two princes of Midian, always named alongside Oreb, during the Midianite invasion of Israel that Gideon defeated. His name means "wolf" according to Easton's Bible Dictionary. After the Midianites were routed, the Ephraimites captured both leaders and killed Zeeb at a winepress that…

Zepho was a son of Eliphaz, Esau's firstborn, and so a grandson of Esau. He is listed with his brothers Teman, Omar, Gatam and Kenaz (Gen 36:11). He also appears among the "dukes", or clan chiefs, descended from Esau, which makes him one of the early tribal leaders of Edom (Gen 36:15). The parallel…

Zerah was a son of Reuel and a grandson of Esau through Esau's wife Bashemath. His brothers were Nahath, Shammah and Mizzah (Gen 36:13; 1 Chr 1:37). He is named among the "dukes," or clan chiefs, descended from Reuel in the land of Edom (Gen 36:17). Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning…

Zeresh was the wife of Haman, the chief official of the Persian king in the book of Esther. When Haman came home angry that Mordecai would not honor him, he gathered his friends and Zeresh (Esth 5:10). She and the friends advised him to build a gallows fifty cubits high and ask the king the next…

Zillah was one of the two wives of Lamech, a descendant of Cain, the other being Adah (Gen 4:19). She bore Tubal-cain, described as an instructor of every craftsman in bronze and iron. Naamah is named as Tubal-cain's sister and is generally taken to be Zillah's daughter as well (Gen 4:22). Zillah…

Zipporah was the wife of Moses and a daughter of Jethro, the priest of Midian, who is also called Reuel (Exod 2:18). After Moses fled Egypt and settled with her family, her father gave her to him in marriage (Exod 2:21). She bore him two sons, Gershom and Eliezer (Exod 2:22; 18:3–4). On the journey…

Zuph, also called Zophai, was a Levite of the Kohathite line and an ancestor of Elkanah, the father of the prophet Samuel. He appears in the genealogy that opens 1 Sam 1:1, where Elkanah of Ramathaim-zophim in the hill country of Ephraim is traced back through Jeroham, Elihu and Tohu to Zuph. The…

Abdon was a judge of Israel, the son of Hillel, from the town of Pirathon. He succeeded Elon as judge (Judg 12:13). The verse between the two cited here, Judg 12:14, says he had forty sons and thirty grandsons who rode on seventy donkeys, and that he judged Israel for eight years. When he died he…

Abdon was a Benjamite named as the firstborn son in the family that settled at Gibeon, listed in the genealogies of 1 Chr 8:30 and 1 Chr 9:36. His father is called Jeiel, "the father of Gibeon," in the surrounding verse (1 Chr 9:35), a name also given as Abiel. His mother was Maachah. His younger…

Abiah was the second son of the prophet Samuel. He and his older brother Joel served as judges in Beersheba, where their father had appointed them (1 Sam 8:2). Abihail was the father of Esther, the Jewish woman who became queen to the Persian king Ahasuerus, and the uncle of Mordecai (Esth 2:15). Since Mordecai is described as Esther's cousin and as having taken her as his own daughter, Abihail had probably died while she was young. Esth 2:7 says that…

Abijah was the mother of King Hezekiah of Judah and the daughter of a man named Zechariah. She is named in 2 Chr 29:1, while the parallel account in 2 Kgs 18:2 gives her name in the shorter form Abi. Her name means "the Lord is my father" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). She was the wife of King Ahaz,…

Abimael was a son of Joktan, named in the Table of Nations in Gen 10:28 and in the matching genealogy in 1 Chr 1:22. He is listed between Obal (called Ebal in Chronicles) and Sheba, ninth of Joktan's thirteen sons. Neighboring verses in these lists, outside the passages given here, make Joktan a…

Abishur was a man of the tribe of Judah who appears only in the genealogy of Jerahmeel's descendants in 1 Chronicles. He was a son of Shammai, son of Onam, and his brother was Nadab (1 Chr 2:28). His wife was Abihail, and she bore him two sons, Ahban and Molid (1 Chr 2:29). The International…

Abital was one of the wives of King David and the mother of his son Shephatiah.
